name: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools
venue: NeurIPS 2023 (Thirty-seventh Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems; poster, https://neurips.cc/virtual/2023/poster/71288; OpenReview id Yacmpz84TH). arXiv preprint arXiv:2302.04761 submitted 9 Feb 2023.
authors_affiliation: Timo Schick, Jane Dwivedi-Yu, Roberto Dessì, Roberta Raileanu, Maria Lomeli, Luke Zettlemoyer, Nicola Cancedda, Thomas Scialom. Primary affiliation: Meta AI Research (FAIR); Roberto Dessì is also affiliated with Universitat Pompeu Fabra. Lead author: Timo Schick (Meta AI Research).
code_url: N/A (no official code/model release from the authors/Meta AI for the paper. Widely used third-party reimplementations exist, e.g. https://github.com/lucidrains/toolformer-pytorch , https://github.com/conceptofmind/toolformer , https://github.com/xrsrke/toolformer , but none is the authors' official implementation) [uncertain]
maintained_repo_url: N/A (no authors-maintained repository, leaderboard, or paper list).
task_domain: tool-use (self-supervised tool/API learning for language models), evaluated on QA / factual lookup (LAMA), math word problems, open-domain QA, multilingual QA, and temporal reasoning. Cross-cutting: it teaches a general LM to decide which API to call, when, with what arguments, and how to use the result.
problem_setting: Offline, single-model, self-supervised setting. A frozen base LM (GPT-J 6.7B; also GPT-2 family 124M-1.6B for scaling) is given only a handful (3-5) of hand-written demonstrations per API. The LM in-context annotates a plain-text corpus (a subset of CCNet) with candidate API calls; the calls are executed against external tools; a self-supervised perplexity-reduction filter (does the API call+result reduce the LM's loss on subsequent tokens) keeps only useful calls; the LM is then finetuned on the API-call-augmented corpus C* with a standard LM objective. At inference the finetuned LM autonomously emits API calls during decoding (interrupting generation when it produces the response token), and downstream tasks are evaluated zero-shot (no in-context task examples). Supervision is only the per-API demonstrations plus the model's own perplexity feedback; no human-annotated tool-use traces and no task-specific tuning.
what_is_retrieved: tools / external API results: at inference the LM invokes external tools (a question-answering system, a Wikipedia/BM25 search engine, a calculator, a calendar, and a machine-translation system) and incorporates their returned text results. For the Wikipedia Search tool specifically, the retrieved unit is short Wikipedia text snippets. The 'retrieved' content the model conditions on is the tool's textual output, not a ranked set of documents per se.
retrieval_grounding: STATIC external corpus / external tools. Tools target fixed external resources: a BM25 retriever over the KILT Wikipedia dump (search engine), an Atlas QA model finetuned on Natural Questions, a Python calculator, a 600M NLLB translation model, and a calendar. There is no agent-written growing episodic memory; the augmented training corpus C* is built offline once and the base LM is frozen aside from finetuning.
completeness_vs_topk_objective: Neither a ranking nor a completeness objective in the retriever sense. The driving objective is perplexity reduction on future tokens: an API call is kept only if L_i^- - L_i^+ >= tau_f (the call+result reduces the LM's weighted cross-entropy loss by at least a threshold). At inference the model issues at most ONE API call per input (a deliberate restriction to avoid loops), so there is no top-k document set and no multi-tool completeness target; tool selection is a single autonomous decision per example.
cbr_cycle_coverage: N/A (not a case-based-reasoning method; no Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain case cycle).
explicit_cbr_grounding: False. The work is framed as self-supervised tool learning / model bootstrapping; it does not cite Aamodt & Plaza or Kolodner and does not describe itself as case-based reasoning.
retrieval_unit: tool-API call and its returned text result. Concretely: a single API call c=(a_c, i_c) (tool name + textual input) linearized with special tokens <API> a_c(i_c) -> r </API>. The returned unit varies by tool: a short answer string (QA), short Wikipedia text snippets (BM25 search over KILT Wikipedia), a numeric result (calculator), the current date string (calendar), or an English translation (NLLB). For the few-shot annotation phase, the in-context unit is 3-5 human-written demonstrations of API usage per tool.
index_source: Offline-induced static construction. The retrievable/usable knowledge is reached through fixed external tools; the central artifact is the augmented corpus C* induced offline by annotating CCNet text with API calls and filtering by perplexity reduction. The base LM is frozen and then finetuned once on C*; nothing is induced or grown at test time. For the search tool, the index is a static BM25 index over the KILT Wikipedia dump.
index_structure_topology: Flat / tool-keyed. The five tools are independent APIs invoked by name (no graph, hierarchy, or clustering of tools). The Wikipedia Search tool uses a flat BM25 lexical index over the KILT Wikipedia dump. There is no learned vector index, no inter-tool dependency graph, and no hierarchical category->tool organization.
retriever_type: Hybrid of off-the-shelf tools plus the LM-as-controller. The LM itself is the generative 'retriever/router' that decides which tool to call and with what argument (tool invocation emitted as special-token text during decoding). The underlying tools include a BM25 lexical retriever (Wikipedia Search over KILT), a retrieval-augmented QA model (Atlas, finetuned on Natural Questions; Atlas-large for data creation, Atlas-xxl at inference), a Python calculator, the fastText language detector + 600M NLLB translator, and a calendar. No dense neural retriever is trained by the authors for tool selection.
retriever_learning_signal: Self-supervised perplexity/LM-feedback. The decision of when/which/how to call a tool is learned by finetuning the LM on API calls that were kept by a self-supervised filter: a call is retained only if including its input and result reduces the weighted cross-entropy loss over subsequent tokens by at least tau_f (L_i^- - L_i^+ >= tau_f). There is no contrastive similarity training, no human relevance labels, no RL, and no downstream-task reward; the only learning signal is the model's own next-token loss reduction (bootstrapping in the STaR / self-training tradition).
query_construction: LM-generated, in-context-conditioned. During data creation, for each API a fixed prompt P(x) instructs the LM to insert API calls into a text x; the LM samples candidate positions (where p_M(<API>) >= tau_s) and then samples up to m candidate calls (tool argument text) at each position. At inference the LM generates the API call argument autonomously as part of decoding, conditioned on the text generated so far. The query (tool argument) is thus composed by the model from its evolving context, not from the raw input verbatim.
query_granularity: Step/position-level within a single text, but capped at one effective call. During corpus annotation, candidate calls are sampled at up to k positions per document (top-k by <API>-token probability, default k=5; k=20 for calculator/MT). At inference, the model can in principle emit a call at any decoding position, but is restricted to AT MOST ONE API call per input. So effectively task-level (one tool decision per example) at test time, position-level during offline data generation.
when_to_retrieve: Adaptive / model-decided (learned router emergent from finetuning). The finetuned LM itself decides when to emit an API call during decoding; there is no fixed schedule. In practice it is one-shot per input (at most one call). The propensity to call is tuned via a modified greedy-decoding rule (emit <API> if it is among the top-k most likely tokens; default k=10 at inference).
retrieval_trigger_signal: Token-level model decision: the model triggers a call when the special <API> token is among the k most likely next tokens (k=10 used at inference vs k=1 = ordinary greedy). During offline annotation, a candidate position is considered only if p_M(<API> | prefix) >= tau_s (default tau_s=0.05; relaxed to 0.0 for calculator/MT). The model is somewhat calibrated at k=1 (it calls APIs preferentially on examples it would otherwise do badly on), though this calibration is lost at higher k.
reranking: None. No reranking stage over tool outputs. During data creation, candidate API calls are filtered by the perplexity-reduction criterion (L_i^- - L_i^+ >= tau_f), which is a thresholded keep/drop filter rather than a learned reranker. The Wikipedia BM25 search returns snippets directly with no second-stage reranker.
retrieved_context_refinement: Minimal / filtering at training-data level. There is no inference-time distillation, decomposition, or compression of tool outputs. The key refinement is the offline self-supervised filter that removes API calls (and results) that do not reduce future-token loss (keeping only useful calls in C*). The authors note that leaving some non-perfectly-filtered noise can be beneficial so the finetuned model does not blindly follow every call result. Tool outputs are inserted into the context as-is at inference.
tool_document_engineering: Per-tool hand-written demonstration prompts (few-shot exemplars), not indexed tool docstrings. Each tool is specified by a natural-language instruction prompt with 3-5 worked input/output examples of how to insert that tool's calls (full prompts in Appendix A.2). There is no synthetic-query augmentation, no expanded summaries, no weighted-field or instruction-tuned tool embeddings; tool 'descriptions' are consumed in-context only during the offline annotation phase, and tool-use ability is then internalized into the LM weights via finetuning.
index_content_separation: N/A. No separation of a lightweight retrievable tool index from heavy on-demand content; tools are invoked directly and return their results inline.
dynamic_index_and_protocol: Static, custom text-API protocol. Each tool is a fixed custom API whose input and output are text sequences, invoked via special <API>...</API> tokens with an explicit ' -> ' result marker; there is no live-synchronized tool catalog, no RapidAPI/RESTful registry, no MCP, and no function-calling schema or CRUD auto-sync. The set of five tools is fixed in advance.
tool_dependency_awareness: No. Tools are sampled and called independently; the method explicitly cannot chain tools (use the output of one tool as input to another) because API calls in the finetuning data are generated independently and at most one call per input is allowed. The paper names this lack of tool chaining and interactivity as a key limitation.
how_retrieved_used: Training signal + prompt augmentation (latent-into-weights). Useful API calls are interleaved into the training text and the LM is FINETUNED on this augmented corpus, internalizing tool use into its weights. At inference the model autonomously generates an API call, the system executes the tool, inserts the result back into the decoding context (after the ' -> ' token), and the LM continues generation conditioned on the tool's returned text. Thus the retrieved tool result directly grounds subsequent token prediction / the final answer.
planning_integration: Inline, per-decoding-step tool invocation within a single generation pass (no explicit planner, no tree search). Tool use is woven into ordinary autoregressive decoding: the model decides during generation to emit a call, the tool result is spliced in, and decoding resumes. There is no separate plan-then-retrieve phase, no multi-step planning loop, and (by design) no chaining of tool calls; effectively a single tool call augments one generation.
reasoning_search_interleaving_granularit: Per-tool-call within a single generation, capped at one call per input. The tool call is interleaved at the token/position where the model emits <API>; decoding is interrupted, the tool runs, and the result is inserted before continuing. Because of the at-most-one-call restriction, this is effectively per-answer (one interleaving point per example) rather than dense per-step interleaving.
adaptation_mechanism: N/A (not a CBR method; no case adaptation). The closest analog is that the finetuned LM internalizes when/how to call tools from the self-generated, perplexity-filtered API-call data.
retrieved_item_representation: Raw text inserted inline. Tool inputs and outputs are linearized as text: <API> tool(argument) -> result </API> (e.g. [QA("...")] -> answer, [Calculator(...)] -> number, [WikiSearch(...)] -> snippet). The model conditions on this raw textual result; there is no distilled strategy, executable program object, or latent-soft-token representation of the tool output.
abstraction_level_of_retrieved_unit: Low / raw factual result. The retrieved unit is a concrete tool output (a fact, a number, a date, a translation, or a short Wikipedia snippet) inserted verbatim, not a distilled strategy, workflow, or guideline.
noise_robustness_mechanism: Self-supervised perplexity filtering of training data plus deliberate retention of mild noise. Only API calls whose results reduce future-token loss are kept in C*, removing most useless/irrelevant calls before finetuning. The authors also observe that not over-filtering (leaving some imperfectly useful calls) helps prevent the finetuned model from blindly trusting every tool result. There is no inference-time relevance evaluator, self-reflection, retriever-aware adversarial training, or distractor-aware SFT; the Wikipedia search results can be poor and the model cannot reformulate/browse (a noted limitation).
memory_type: none (no persistent episodic/skill/workflow/graph memory). Tool-use competence is stored in the finetuned LM weights (parametric), not in an external retrievable memory store that grows or is queried at test time.
write_back: False (no test-time memory write-back). New experiences/cases are not stored into an external memory during deployment. (Offline, useful API calls are written into the training corpus C* and then baked into weights via finetuning, but this is a one-time offline data-construction step, not online write-back.)
online_growth: No. The augmented corpus C* is constructed once offline and the model is finetuned once; nothing grows at test time. The base LM is frozen apart from the single finetuning pass, and the tool index (e.g. BM25 Wikipedia) is static.
write_back_trigger: Never at deployment. During offline data construction, the 'write' (keeping an API call in C*) is triggered when the call+result reduces future-token loss by at least the threshold (perplexity-improvement / on-usefulness trigger), i.e. a self-supervised keep criterion, not a deployment-time memory write or a success/failure or reflective trigger.
failure_experience_usage: Success/usefulness-only, no failure memory. The filter keeps only API calls that DECREASE perplexity (useful calls); calls that do not reduce loss are discarded, not stored as negative/failure examples. There is no contrastive use of failed calls and no corrective failure-rule store. (The retained mild noise is incidental, not an explicit failure-experience mechanism.)
memory_evolution_update: N/A / append-only at the data-construction level. The augmented corpus C* is assembled once (useful calls appended/interleaved into texts) and never mutated, deduped, or refined after writing; tool-use knowledge is then frozen into the finetuned weights. No delta-update, refine-overwrite, or forget-prune of stored entries.
retrieval_as_learned_policy: Partially. Tool invocation is NOT a fixed similarity top-k; the LM learns (via self-supervised finetuning on perplexity-filtered data) an emergent policy for when/which/how to call a tool. However, it is not an RL/value-based or M-MDP policy and not a trained ranking retriever; it is a generative decision internalized by language-model finetuning, with the trigger modulated at decode time by the top-k <API>-token rule.
cross_agent_or_cross_framework_sharing: No. Single model, single-agent; tool-use ability is private to the finetuned LM. No memory or experience sharing across agents or frameworks.
benchmarks: LAMA (SQuAD, Google-RE, T-REx subsets; factual cloze completion); math word problems ASDiv, SVAMP, MAWPS; open-domain QA WebQS (Web Questions), Natural Questions (NQ), TriviaQA; multilingual QA MLQA (Es, De, Hi, Vi, Zh, Ar); temporal datasets TEMPLAMA and a newly introduced DATESET (~9,400 templated date-reasoning queries). Language-modeling perplexity on WikiText(-103) and a CCNet validation subset. Base models: GPT-J 6.7B (main) and GPT-2 family (124M/355M/775M/1.6B) for scaling.
benchmark_family: QA (LAMA factual lookup, WebQS, NQ, TriviaQA), multilingual QA (MLQA), math word problems (ASDiv/SVAMP/MAWPS), temporal/knowledge reasoning (TEMPLAMA, DATESET), and language modeling perplexity (WikiText, CCNet). Spans the QA and tool-augmented-reasoning families; not the agentic web/embodied/tool-retrieval (ToolBench-style) benchmark families.
baselines: Same-size GPT-J variants: GPT-J (vanilla, no finetuning), GPT-J + CC (GPT-J finetuned on the same CCNet subset C WITHOUT API calls), Toolformer (disabled) (the Toolformer model but with API calls turned off at decoding), and Toolformer (full). Larger LM baselines: OPT (66B) and GPT-3 (175B, text-davinci-002 era). For MLQA, additional 'AllEn' upper-bound rows give GPT-J and GPT-3 English contexts+questions. Related self-supervised tool-learning method TALM (Parisi et al., 2022) is discussed as the closest prior work but not directly tabulated.
key_metrics: Zero-shot downstream accuracy: for LAMA/TEMPLAMA, whether the correct word is in the first 5 predicted words; for QA datasets, whether the correct answer is in the first ~20 (10 for MLQA) predicted words; for math benchmarks, whether the predicted number matches. Language-modeling perplexity on WikiText and CCNet. Plus diagnostic statistics: fraction of examples where each tool is called.
headline_result: Toolformer (based on a 6.7B GPT-J) substantially improves zero-shot performance and, on several tasks, outperforms the much larger OPT (66B) and GPT-3 (175B). Examples from the paper: LAMA T-REx 53.5 vs GPT-3 (175B) 39.8 and vs best same-size baseline ~34.9 (+18.6 over best GPT-J baseline); LAMA SQuAD 33.8 vs GPT-3 26.8; math MAWPS 44.0 / ASDiv 40.4 / SVAMP 29.4, each more than doubling the no-tool baselines and clearly beating GPT-3 (19.8/14.0/10.0) and OPT-66B. Tool calls are issued autonomously (e.g. QA tool used for 98.1% of LAMA examples, calculator for 97.9% of math examples), and adding API calls does not increase language-modeling perplexity.
ablations: (1) Toolformer vs Toolformer(disabled) isolates the value of actually calling tools at inference: e.g. math performance more than doubles when calls are enabled; LAMA T-REx jumps from 34.9 (disabled) to 53.5 (enabled). (2) GPT-J + CC vs Toolformer(disabled) shows finetuning on API-augmented text (even without calling tools) gives modest gains (the model internalizes some skill, especially math). (3) Decoding-strategy ablation (Table 9): varying k in the top-k <API> rule from k=1 (greedy, calls on 40.3% of T-REx / 8.5% of WebQS examples) to k=10 (98.1% / 100%); higher k increases call frequency and performance but loses the k=1 calibration. (4) Scaling-laws ablation (Sec 4.4, GPT-2 124M-1.6B + GPT-J): the ability to benefit from tools EMERGES only around 775M parameters; smaller models gain little, and a large with-vs-without-tool gap persists even for the largest model. (5) Data-quality analysis (Table 10): high L_i^- - L_i^+ filter scores correspond to intuitively useful calls. (6) Filtering-threshold tau_f statistics (Table 2) show the number of retained examples per tool.
evaluation_decoupling: No. The paper does not report intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k / nDCG / completeness) separately. Evaluation is end-to-end zero-shot task accuracy plus perplexity; retrieval/tool quality is examined only via tool-call frequencies and qualitative data-quality analysis.
process_vs_outcome_metrics: Primarily outcome metrics (zero-shot task accuracy, perplexity). Some process-level diagnostics are reported: the fraction of examples each tool is called on (e.g. 98.1% QA, 97.9% calculator, 0.2% calendar on TEMPLAMA, 54.8% calendar on DATESET), calibration analysis at k=1, and qualitative inspection of the usefulness of generated API calls.
cost_efficiency_tradeoff: Emphasizes parameter efficiency: a 6.7B GPT-J Toolformer matches or beats OPT-66B and GPT-3-175B on tool-amenable tasks, and adding tool calls does not increase LM perplexity. The method is sample-INefficient at data-creation time: processing more than a million documents yields only a few thousand useful calculator API examples (Table 2: e.g. 994 calculator examples at tau_f=1.0). Training uses up to 25k examples per API, max seq length 1,024, effective batch size 128, DeepSpeed ZeRO-3, 8x NVIDIA A100 40GB (BF16), up to 2k steps. At inference at most one API call per input is allowed; decoding is interrupted once to run the tool. No explicit per-query API-dollar/latency table is reported.
context_budget_and_selection_count: Few-shot per-tool demonstrations (3-5 hand-written examples per API) in the annotation prompt. Data-creation hyperparameters: top k=5 candidate positions per text (k=20 for calculator/MT), up to m=5 candidate calls per position (m=10 for calculator/MT), tau_s=0.05 (0.0 for calculator/MT), tau_f=1.0 (0.5 for calculator/MT). Inference: emit <API> if among top k=10 tokens; AT MOST ONE API call per input. Tool outputs are inserted inline with no explicit token-budget cap or truncation beyond the tool's own short return (e.g. Wikipedia snippets).
benchmark_construction_and_size: Introduces DATESET, a new temporal-reasoning benchmark: ~9,400 queries generated from 7 template families (Table 11) populated by randomly selecting 500 'current dates' and associated random past/future dates within a four-year range (plus US federal holidays), where knowing the current date is required to answer; verifiability is exact (templated, deterministic answers). Toolformer scores 27.3 on DATESET (using the calendar tool for 54.8% of examples) vs <=5.9 for all baselines including GPT-3 (175B) at 0.8, signaling the task isolates calendar-tool utility. Other benchmarks are pre-existing (LAMA, ASDiv/SVAMP/MAWPS, WebQS/NQ/TriviaQA, MLQA, TEMPLAMA, WikiText, CCNet).
builds_on: Self-training / bootstrapping for self-improvement, especially STaR (Zelikman et al., 2022) and dataset-generation-from-LMs (Schick & Schütze 2021b; Honovich et al. 2022 Unnatural Instructions; Wang et al. 2022 Self-Instruct); in-context learning of GPT-3 (Brown et al., 2020). Base LM GPT-J 6B (Wang & Komatsuzaki, 2021) and GPT-2 (Radford et al., 2019). Tools build on the Atlas retrieval-augmented QA model (Izacard et al., 2022) finetuned on Natural Questions, a BM25 retriever (Robertson et al., 1995) over the KILT Wikipedia dump (Petroni et al., 2021), the 600M NLLB translator (Costa-jussà et al., 2022), and the fastText classifier (Joulin et al., 2016). Training corpus CCNet (Wenzek et al., 2020).
contrasts_with: Closest prior work TALM (Parisi et al., 2022), which uses a similar self-supervised objective but only in task-specific finetuned settings; tool-use approaches relying on large human supervision (WebGPT, Nakano et al. 2021; Komeili et al. 2022; LaMDA/Thoppilan et al. 2022) or on task-specific few-shot prompting that presupposes which tool to use (PAL/Gao et al. 2022; Lazaridou et al. 2022; ReAct/Yao et al. 2022). Also contrasted with retrieval-augmented pretraining methods (REALM/Guu et al. 2020, RETRO/Borgeaud et al. 2021, Atlas/Izacard et al. 2022) that always inject retrieved text regardless of usefulness, whereas Toolformer learns to ask for the right information for itself.
lineage: Group E (tool use). A foundational self-supervised tool-learning method: it teaches a general LM to autonomously decide when/which/how to call external APIs by bootstrapping training data via perplexity-filtered self-annotation, in contrast to prompt-based interleaved tool-use agents (ReAct) and human-supervised tool agents (WebGPT). A direct precursor to subsequent tool-augmented LMs and function-calling / tool-retrieval lines of work.
